topStories.headline: Gene Friend Rec Center Set to Reopen Aug. 13 After $59M Rebuild
topStories.dek: SoMa's only indoor recreation center will finally open its doors after more than two years of construction, just in time for the new school year.
topStories.body:
After closing for demolition in February 2024, the Gene Friend Recreation Center at 270 Sixth St. is scheduled to reopen on Thursday, August 13 — a date that San Francisco Recreation and Parks announced on July 22. The new 25,000-square-foot facility replaces the old center with 50 percent more space, designed to serve children, families, and seniors in one of the city's most densely populated and underserved neighborhoods.

The $59 million project, designed by Mark Cavagnero Associates in partnership with Kuth Ranieri Architects, includes a gymnasium with two full-size basketball courts surrounded by expansive windows for natural light, a modern exercise area, two multi-purpose rooms, a kitchenette, and a new exterior playground on Harriet Street. The grand opening is scheduled for 11:30 a.m. at the facility's new Harriet Street address (77 Harriet St.).

The closure hit SoMa hard. With hundreds of children and teens relying on the center for after-school programs and supervised activity in a dense urban core, the neighborhood has leaned on Victoria Manalo Draves Park and outdoor courts as a stopgap. The San Francisco Recreation and Park Department also acquired an adjacent parcel at 240 Sixth Street in November 2024, positioning the city for a possible long-term expansion of the facility.

The reopening arrives just before the start of the San Francisco Unified School District school year, giving local families a new indoor hub as summer programs wind down.

topStories.headline: Prologis Railyards Megaproject Moves Through Planning: 2,500 Homes, 850-Foot Tower Proposed at 4th & King
topStories.dek: A sweeping redevelopment proposal for the Caltrain railyards between SoMa and Mission Bay has entered environmental review, with a buildout that could reshape the neighborhood for decades.
topStories.body:
Developer Prologis submitted an application to San Francisco's Planning Department in March to transform the 20-acre Caltrain railyards at Fourth and King streets into a dense mixed-use district — one of the most ambitious post-pandemic development proposals in the city's pipeline. The project envisions up to 2,500 housing units, approximately 4 million square feet of commercial office space, retail, and potentially a hotel, all anchored by an 850-foot tower rising directly above a rebuilt Caltrain station.

The site — currently the active northern terminus and maintenance yard for Caltrain — spans the blocks between Fourth and Seventh streets and King and Townsend streets. Prologis owns the land beneath while Caltrain holds a perpetual operational easement, a legal arrangement that will govern how tracks, platforms, and new buildings are integrated. The company says it anticipates a construction timeline of 15 to 20 years at full buildout, with the first phase covering roughly 2.5 million square feet.

For SoMa and Mission Bay residents, the stakes are significant. As the Potrero View noted in its July 2026 issue, the active rail yard effectively acts as a physical barrier between SoMa, Showplace Square, and Mission Bay. Caltrain's public information officer, Dan Lieberman, told the View that the project is not proposing any changes to Caltrain service, though temporary schedule changes could be necessary during construction.

The proposal has now entered environmental review, which the San Francisco Planning Department estimates could take up to two years. A development agreement process will run in parallel. Residents and neighborhood groups in Mission Bay and SoMa have begun weighing in, with some calling for the project to prioritize child-friendly design and high-quality architecture befitting the waterfront location.

topStories.headline: Pokémon World Championships Coming to Moscone Center and Chase Center, Aug. 28–30
topStories.dek: For the first time, the Pokémon World Championships' grand finals will move to Chase Center in Mission Bay, while the Moscone Center hosts the inaugural PokémonXP fan festival.
topStories.body:
San Francisco's SoMa and Mission Bay neighborhoods will be buzzing with trainers, collectors, and fans from around the world at the end of August when the 2026 Pokémon World Championships take over two of the cluster's biggest venues. Preliminary rounds and the new PokémonXP fan convention will run at the Moscone Center (747 Howard St., SoMa) from August 28 through 30, while Championship Sunday's grand finals will make history by moving to Chase Center (1 Warriors Way, Mission Bay) on August 30.

This year's event carries extra weight: it marks the 30th anniversary of the Pokémon franchise and features the competitive debut of Pokémon Champions, a new dedicated battle game released in April 2026. PokémonXP — the event's new open-to-everyone fan festival — will include panels, workshops, special guests, cosplay competitions, autograph sessions, and a pop-up Pokémon Center store with exclusive merchandise.

The San Francisco Giants are also joining in: the team is hosting a Pokémon Worlds Night at Oracle Park on August 27, with Pikachu scheduled to throw the first pitch and a special Pikachu-themed jersey available for fans. Both Moscone Center and Chase Center are accessible via Muni Metro, BART, and Bay Wheels bike share.

Organizers expect tens of thousands of visitors, which is likely to bring increased foot traffic and economic activity to nearby SoMa restaurants, bars, and hotels throughout the weekend.

moreNews.headline: Esprit Park Renovation Celebrated — UCSF Investment Breathes New Life Into Dogpatch Green Space
moreNews.body: Dogpatch's Esprit Park completed an $8.5 million renovation earlier this year, culminating in a February 2025 ribbon-cutting that drew city leaders and longtime residents. The project was funded through a roughly $4.1 million grant from UCSF, approximately $3.6 million in Eastern Neighborhoods Development Impact Fees, and an additional $835,000 UCSF grant managed by the Dogpatch & NW Potrero Hill Green Benefit District. The park — originally built as a private corporate park by the Esprit clothing company in 1982 and transferred to the city in 2001 — was redesigned by Fletcher Studio Landscape Architecture & Urban Design and now offers improved safety, new amenities, and expanded programming space for a neighborhood that has grown significantly denser in recent years. UCSF's investment in Esprit Park is part of more than $10 million in contributions the university has made in Dogpatch and surrounding neighborhoods.

moreNews.headline: SoMa West Residents File State Complaint Over Concentration of Homeless Services
moreNews.body: The SoMa West Neighborhood Association, which represents more than 200 city residents, submitted a formal complaint to the California Department of Housing and Community Development earlier this year, alleging that San Francisco has disproportionately directed homeless resources and supportive housing into the South of Market neighborhood. The city's Office of Economic and Workforce Development noted that the Office of Homelessness and Supportive Housing awarded Abode Property Management $734,827 annually for SoMa Ambassadors. Board member Alex Ludlum said the city is adding security coverage but that residents believe systemic change is needed, not incremental adjustments. The complaint remains under review.

moreNews.headline: Harmonic Brewing Settles Into Thrive City Home After Dogpatch Closure
moreNews.body: Harmonic Brewing has fully transitioned from its original Dogpatch warehouse taproom to its current location at Thrive City, the plaza surrounding Chase Center in Mission Bay. The independent brewery — known for small-batch Kölsches, sours, and IPAs — now operates Tues.–Fri. 3–9 PM, Sat. noon–9 PM, and Sun. noon–8 PM, with extended hours before and after Warriors games and events. The Dogpatch location, which served the neighborhood since 2015, permanently closed in late 2023.
